newsitem.title: FRANCE: France aims to make a big splash with telecom sale.
newsitem.headline: France aims to make a big splash with telecom sale.

text.p: France wants to make the sale of France Telecom the biggest market flotation ever and use the partial privatisation as a means of promoting popular shareholding, Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday.

France's centre-right government hopes the France Telecom sale will have the same kind of popular response as the Deutsche Telekom flotation in Germany in November 1996 and entice households to invest in shares in the way Britain's wave of privatisations under Margaret Thatcher created a culture of popular capitalism.
France will sell between 30 and 50 billion francs of
France Telecom shares in the coming months, starting with a three-week reservation period for private individuals on May 6 and the official sale from May 27.

The reservation system is designed to fuel interest in the sale, which Arthuis described as "the biggest flotation ever carried out in France". The record currently stands at 35.7 billion francs ($6.3 billion) for Elf-Aquitaine in 1994.
"The reservation system will be at the heart of the publicity campaign," Arthuis said "The aim is to get as much of the public involved as possible."
The new reservation system -- which will require a modification to a 1993 law -- will allow people to reserve shares at their bank before a firm price is set.
They will then have the right but not the obligation to buy France Telecom shares in the float.
On Wednesday, France Telecom chairman Michel Bon said he hoped to have more than two million shareholders and said that surveys had shown there was "tremendous interest" in the shares.
The sale campaign started on Thursday with a day-long briefing for financial analysts and the airing of commercials on radio stations urging people to reserve telecom shares at their banks in May.
French newspapers were mildly positive about the operation.
Editorialist Patrick Lamm of the Les Echos financial daily said that the government must not fail in the sale because telecom was "the last milk-cow" left to sell.

He added that while the telecoms industry had good prospects and the share market was doing fine, the appetite of UK and U.S. investors might be limited by any government faux pas in dealing with Renault job cuts or the Eramet nickel mine in New Caledonia.

David Barroux of La Tribune Desfosses warned that while France Telecom's prospects were bright, the company would have to successfully manage the change from a state-controlled monopoly to a private firm in a ruthless competitive market.

The Communist daily L'Humanite noted, however, that now that the market was looking up the government had decided "to abandon public control of a sector of the future and throw on the market a part of the national potential".
A price range will be set for the shares during the evening of May 5, and the reservation period will last until May 26.
The actual market flotation will begin on May 27 and close on June 3 with the first share trading in New York and Paris scheduled for June 9.
